title: Singapore Airlines Keeps Door Open for Further Capital Injections Into Air India
excerpt: The carrier said its board has set no predetermined investment limit for Air India, calling the 25.1% stake a cornerstone of its multi-hub growth strategy even as the Indian airline posted a ₹26,400 crore loss in FY26.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Singapore Airlines is open to further capital investments in Air India without a set limit.
  • Air India reported a ₹26,400 crore loss in FY26, impacting Singapore Airlines' profits significantly.
  • SIA CEO emphasizes a long-term strategy for Air India's recovery, citing external challenges.
  • Tata Sons and SIA invested ₹9,558 crore in Air India in FY25, with SIA holding a 25.1% stake.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=Fl7EGnxQegA

No Cap on Future Funding

Singapore Airlines has signalled its willingness to pump more capital into Tata Group-owned Air India, telling investors that its board has not fixed any predetermined limit on future investments in the loss-making Indian carrier.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZEZiB8jGOo/

"The board will carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the Group's other capital requirements and Air India's business strategy," Singapore Airlines said in responses shared with the Securities Investors Association (Singapore) ahead of its annual general meeting.

The comments came as Air India's financial performance continued to weigh heavily on SIA's books. Air India reported a net loss of ₹26,400 crore ($2.6 billion) in FY26—driven by fleet modernisation costs, the Vistara merger integration, Pakistan airspace closures, and rupee depreciation against the US dollar. SIA recognised a share of loss of S$330 million from its Air India stake, compared with a share of profit of S$48 million from Vistara the previous year. SIA's own net profit fell 56% in FY26.

The Long Game

SIA Chief Executive Goh Choon Phong, who also serves on Air India's board, has been candid about the timeline. "It is going to be a long game. There will be no short cuts," he said during a post-results conference call in May. He attributed Air India's losses largely to external factors—Pakistan's continued airspace closure, which forces longer routing for key international flights, and the weak Indian rupee.

"This is a market which holds tremendous potential and is even more obvious today."

— Goh Choon Phong, CEO, Singapore Airlines

Despite the red ink, Goh pointed to tangible progress: Air India's net promoter score has improved by 50 points, training and in-flight services have been upgraded, and airport lounges have been refurbished. SIA has seconded two senior executives to Air India—Captain Basil Kwauk as chief operations officer and Jeremy Yew Jin Kit as head of engineering—to support the transformation effort.

Strategic Rationale

Singapore Airlines described its 25.1% stake in the enlarged Air India Group as a cornerstone of its multi-hub strategy. As a city-state with no domestic aviation market, Singapore depends on international traffic. India's fast-growing domestic aviation sector—one of the world's largest by passenger volume—offers SIA access to traffic flows it cannot generate from its home hub alone.

The airline noted it is the only non-Indian carrier with a direct equity stake in India's aviation market. Each of SIA's international investments—including past stakes in Air New Zealand, Virgin Atlantic, and Virgin Australia—is evaluated independently based on long-term growth potential, strategic fit, operating environment, and risk profile, the company said.

Tata Sons and SIA together invested ₹9,558 crore in Air India in FY25, with Tata contributing ₹3,225 crore and SIA ₹6,333 crore. In March 2026 alone, Tata injected another ₹3,225 crore and SIA added ₹1,081 crore through preferential share allotments.

What's Next

Air India's transformation plan—originally conceived as a five-year overhaul when the Tata Group acquired the airline in January 2022—is roughly halfway through execution. The carrier continues to face headwinds including high fuel prices, supply-chain disruptions, and the aftermath of the AI-171 accident. For the Indian diaspora, which has long relied on Air India for direct connectivity between India and the world, the airline's trajectory under Tata-SIA stewardship will determine whether improved service and expanded routes become permanent fixtures or remain aspirational targets.
